rationale: A wins because it knows where the cliff edge is and stops before walking the founder over it. Its strongest line, "The number Toast won't give you: default rates on its restaurant cash advances," is adversarial but grounded and paired with the filing check that keeps it honest. B has sharper spread, but "Toast reached profitability by selling loans, not hardware" is a causal claim the fact block does not support, and "loans" is already sloppy on a merchant-cash-advance story. That is how a decent angle set gets a reporter to stop trusting the rest of it.
gaps_in_A: "Toast crosses 120,000 restaurant locations as it pivots from hardware to fintech margins" slightly overstates the move; the update supports bundling and higher-margin fintech, not a full pivot.
A leaves a useful markets/data angle half-submerged inside the category angle instead of making the profitability-quality question its own clean lane.

"The prevailing belief is that a newly profitable, publicly traded platform lending against its own customers' sales has a clean, well-understood book" needs a cited belief; A asks for verification later, but the frame itself is still asserted.
gaps_in_B: "Toast reached profitability by selling loans, not hardware" is the big sin: unsupported causation, wrong instrument language, and too much confidence in one headline.

"comes out automatically through the same system that takes the payments" and "the operator never writes a check" are plausible, but not in the update; do not decorate mechanics you have not confirmed.
"restaurants — an industry with well-known failure rates" imports an outside trope without sourcing it from the fact block.
"concentrated supplier markets" and the lock-in frame may be interesting, but the update only gives bundling and fee complaints; the market-power claim needs evidence before it can carry an angle.
